strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing proactive interference in long-context LLMs with clear presentation and intuitive framing
Strong empirical results on NeedleBench Multi-Needle Reasoning with consistent improvements across all three models (Claude: +27, GPT-4.1: +23, DeepSeek: +8 points)
Practical zero-shot approach leveraging LLMs' inherent tool-calling capabilities without requiring fine-tuning
Evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art models (Claude-4-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3) demonstrates some generalization
Interesting perspective positioning ACM as complementary to external memory and context window expansion
weaknesses: Incomplete evaluation: promised multi-turn RL training results are missing and explicitly stated as 'ongoing work,' making the paper feel premature
Severely limited benchmark scope: only 2 information-sparse benchmarks evaluated; no general long-context tasks, QA, summarization, or real-world applications tested

Inconsistent and problematic PI-LLM results: DeepSeek-V3 shows overall degradation (-5.93%), and dramatic drops at specific settings (Claude: 99.87%→79.57%, DeepSeek: 100%→53.48%) indicate tool use is actively harmful in some cases without adequate explanation

No computational cost analysis despite acknowledging that ACM invalidates KV cache mechanisms; missing critical latency, token overhead, and computational measurements essential for practical deployment
No comparison with related context compression methods (LongLLMLingua, ReComp, etc.) or simple baselines; missing ablation studies to identify which tools matter and when they should be used

Methodological concerns: tool_choice='required' forces suboptimal tool use; generalization relies on transfer from other domains rather than ACM-specific learning; task-specific tool preferences (fragment/fold vs. search) suggest lack of general solution
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars despite observed performance volatility; failure analysis missing for PI-LLM degradation cases

Missing detailed reproducibility information: exact prompts not provided, embedding model specifications incomplete ('OpenAI embeddings' undefined), no code release mentioned, tool implementation details sparse

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and grounds proactive interference as a fundamental LLM limitation with strong cognitive and empirical foundations
Principled tool design with four coherent design principles (deterministic, cognitively aligned, structurally preserving, reversible) resulting in thoughtful implementation
Novel RL contribution: conditional trajectory collection with incremental loss assignment is a technically sound solution to training agents whose tools modify context non-monotonically
Comprehensive evaluation on five diverse benchmarks (PI-LLM, NeedleBench, MRCR, LongBenchV2, FRAMES) with three frontier models and custom RL results
Insightful analysis of unguided tool use (Section 4.1, Figure 3) identifying three fundamental challenges in natural tool adoption
Strong mechanistic evidence: value-specific attention analysis (Section 4.3) demonstrates 93.5% of key-value pairs improve with folding (mean +9.87%, p<0.001, R²=0.97)
Substantial context reduction of 76-89% across benchmarks (Figure 6) with practical efficiency implications
Excellent reproducibility documentation: detailed prompts, hyperparameters, tool schemas, and training configuration in appendices
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on prompt engineering undermines generality: benchmark-specific prompts show dramatic gains (e.g., PI-LLM NeedleBench 72%→89.9%), making it unclear how much improvement comes from tools vs. prompts; no ablation isolating these contributions

Generalization failures: DeepSeek-V3 shows negative improvement (-0.12 average) on PI-LLM with ACM tools, indicating poor cross-model generalization; complex reasoning tasks (LongBenchV2, FRAMES) show minimal gains (±1.5 points)

Weak baseline comparisons: RAG uses only BM25 (no learned embeddings, known to be weak); no comparison to strong context compression methods (LLMLingua, SnapKV, KVQuant, Scissorhands) despite citing them; limits conclusions about relative performance

RL results only on custom M3 model (13B), not on frontier models where impact would matter most; requires 128 H800 GPUs, limiting reproducibility; unclear if RL would help models that fail naturally (e.g., DeepSeek-V3)

Training/evaluation mismatch: RL trained on synthetic tasks (BABILong, GSM-Infinite) but evaluated on different benchmarks; transfer learning is imperfect, and 'autonomous discovery' claim overstates what model learns
Missing ablation studies: no isolation of individual tools' contributions; unclear which of six tools are necessary for gains on each benchmark or if some are redundant
Incomplete cost analysis: end-to-end latency/throughput not measured; tool execution overhead (e.g., LLM summarization calls) not quantified; no computational cost comparison to baselines

Tool design limitations: exact keyword search is brittle vs. semantic search; summarization quality depends on the LLM itself (circular dependency); claims about cognitive alignment lack empirical validation

Limited applicability to realistic tasks: PI-LLM and NeedleBench are semi-synthetic benchmarks specifically designed to stress test; FRAMES and LongBenchV2 (more realistic) show minimal or negative gains, questioning real-world utility

Overclaimed contributions: 'cognitive agency' and 'self-evolution' framing not well-supported; RL novelty is primarily conditional trajectory collection; GSPO itself is prior work (Zheng et al., 2025)
Reproducibility concerns: M3 model is custom-trained with unclear code/weights availability; frontier model results rely on external APIs; RL-trained Sculptor-M3-RL model not provided
Presentation issues: Figures 3 and 5 are difficult to read; distinction between ACM paradigm and Sculptor implementation could be clearer; some notation introduced but not consistently used

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing proactive interference with clear cognitive psychology parallels
Principled tool design with four sound design principles leading to practical, implementable tools
Valuable empirical insights in Section 4.1 analyzing why unguided tool use fails, providing clear guidance for future work
Strong experimental results on key benchmarks: +27 pts on NeedleBench, +73% on 5-needle tasks, 81.4% context reduction
Novel RL training approach with conditional trajectory collection and incremental loss assignment that elegantly handles non-monotonic context evolution
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple models (Claude-4-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3, M3) and diverse benchmarks
Solid value-specific attention analysis with 93.5% of pairs showing improved attention allocation when using folding
Excellent reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameters, training configurations, and complete tool schemas in appendix
weaknesses: Zero-shot performance heavily depends on hand-crafted benchmark-specific prompts, limiting practical applicability; suboptimal guidance shows models struggle (72% vs 89.9%)
Weak baseline comparisons: RAG uses only BM25 without dense embeddings; missing comparisons to LLMLingua and modern retrieval systems; MemAgent on different foundations
Inconsistent results across models: DeepSeek-V3 shows -0.12 average on PI-LLM, indicating non-universal applicability; minimal investigation into failure cases
Poor performance on reasoning-heavy tasks: LongBenchV2 (+1.5 pts, still 34.5%) and FRAMES (-0.6 pts, decreased); suggests scope limited to retrieval rather than complex reasoning
Limited generalization: RL training on simple benchmarks (BABILong, GSM-Infinite) shows modest transfer to complex benchmarks, with no evidence of cross-domain generalization
Moderate attention improvements: mean 9.87% with 6.5% negative cases and high variance; statistically significant but not dramatic
Low tool design novelty: fragmentation, folding, and search are straightforward; primary contribution is application rather than methodology
Arbitrary experimental choices without justification: 20-tool budget, training dataset selection, simplistic reward design lacking sensitivity analysis
Significant reproducibility barriers: M3 requires 128 H800 GPU pre-training; code/data release not mentioned; results limited to text-only long-context tasks
